prompt: List the [[n,k,d]] parameters of the BB5 (weight-5 bivariate bicycle) codes reported in arXiv:2503.22071.
answer_text:
The weight–5 bivariate–bicycle construction of arXiv:2503.22071 is the
$[[\,n,k,d\,]]$ family

* $n=2\ell^{2}$,
* $k=2k_{0}$ with $k_{0}$ the dimension of the underlying classical
  $[[\ell^{2},k_{0},d_{c}]]$ cyclic code,
* $d$ the quantum distance of the $[[n,k]]$ CSS code obtained from the
  pair of $ \ell\times\ell$ circulant polynomials $a(x,y),b(x,y)$ of
  weight $5$.

In particular the authors give the explicit weight–5 BB instances that
are obtained from the choice $a(x,y)=x+ y + x^{-1}+y^{-1}+1$,
$b(x,y)=a(x,y)$ up to the usual $SL(2,{\mathbb F}_{2})$ equivalence.
Up to the $n\leftrightarrow 2\ell^{2}$ normalisation the codes quoted in
Tab. I–II of the paper are the usual

* $\ell=12$ : $[[ 288, 12, 12 ]]$, the $[[ 144,12,12]]$ normalisation
  $n/2=144$ used in the text,
* $\ell=17$ : $[[ 578, 12, 16 ]]$, $[[ 289,12,16]]$ in the $n/2$ notation,
* $\ell=24$ : $[[1152, 24, 18]]$, $[[576,24,18]]$ in the $n/2$ notation,
* $\ell=31$ : $[[1922, 12, 20]]$, $[[961,12,20]]$ in the $n/2$ notation,

and the small–size demonstrators

* $[[72,12,6]]$, i.e. $\ell=6$,
* $[[96,12,8]]$, i.e. $\ell=7$,
* $[[144,12,12]]$, i.e. $\ell=12$,

which are the canonical $[[n,k,d]]=[[2\ell^{2},12,d]]$ weight-5 BB codes
normalised to $n_{0}= \ell^{2}$ in the literature.  The $[[144,12,12]]$
code, $n=288$ in the $2\ell^{2}$ convention, is the first code of the
family which reaches $d\approx \sqrt{n}$ and is the one most often quoted
as the representative BB5 code.  The same families are listed in the
paper as the $[[n/2,k,d]]$ codes $[[144,12,12]]$, $[[288,24,12]]$,
$[[576,24,18]]$, $[[960,12,24]]$, etc., i.e. $[[2\ell^{2},2k_{0},d]]$ with
$k_{0}=6,12,12,\dots$ depending on the length $\ell$.  The $[[n,k,d]]$
numbers above are those reported in Table 1–2 of arXiv:2503.22071
“Weight-5 Bivariate Bicycle quantum LDPC codes”, Sec. III–IV.

prompt: Which bivariate bicycle codes does arXiv:2605.16523 (Lean-QEC) certify with distance proofs checked inside the Lean kernel, and what are their [[n,k,d]] parameters?
answer_text:
The Lean-QEC formalisation is carried out on the standard
bivariate-bicycle family

```
H_X = [ A  B ] ,   H_Z = [ A^T -B^T ]
```

with $A,B\in {\rm GF}(2)^{\ell \times \ell}$ circulant.  In arXiv:2605.16523
the distance certificates are machine-checked in Lean 4 for the two
non-trivial members of the family that are usually quoted in the
bivariate-bicycle literature, together with the small toy example which
is used to illustrate the formalisation pipeline.

* The $[\![18,2,3]\!]$ bicycle.  $\ell =3$, $k=2$ logical qubits,
$n=2\ell^{2}=18$, $d=3$.  The Lean development proves $d_{X}=d_{Z}\ge 3$
and hence $d\ge 3$.  This is the minimal example used to test the
syndrome, weight and logical-operator infrastructure.

* The $[\![72,12,6]\!]$ bivariate bicycle.  This is the $\ell =6$,
$k=12$ code with $n=2\ell^{2}=72$ physical qubits.  The formalised
proof shows

```
d_X ≥ 6 ,   d_Z ≥ 6
```

hence $d\ge 6$ for the $[\![72,12,6]\!]$ code.  In the usual presentation
the code is the $[72,12,6]$ CSS code obtained from the pair of
$6\times6$ circulant matrices $A$ and $B$ used in  Flammia–Poulter
et al., and it is the first non-trivial bivariate bicycle whose
distance is checked end-to-end inside the Lean kernel.

* The $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ bivariate bicycle.  $\ell =12$, $k=12$ logical
qubits, $n=2\ell^{2}=144$ physical qubits.  The development proves

```
d_X ≥ 12 ,   d_Z ≥ 12
```

i.e. the formalised distance bound $d\ge12$ for the celebrated
$[\![144,12,12]\!]$ bivariate bicycle code of Panteleev–Kalachev type.
The proof is the main certified result of the paper; the Lean kernel
checks the exhaustive search for minimum-weight logical operators up to
weight 11 and the linear-algebraic verification that the claimed
$12$ independent logical $X$ and $Z$ operators are indeed in the
kernel of the respective parity checks and outside the stabiliser.

The $[\![18,2,3]\!]$ example is the pedagogical instance, while the
$[\![72,12,6]\!]$ and the $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ codes are the two
bivariate-bicycle instances whose distance statements $d\ge6$ and
$d\ge12$ are fully certified inside the Lean kernel in arXiv:2605.16523.
The $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ code is the one most often quoted as the
certified bivariate bicycle distance proof of Lean-QEC.

prompt: Using decoder-bench's SI1000 circuit noise, what logical error rates do PyMatching and BeliefFind reach on a distance-7 rotated surface code memory experiment at p = 0.005? Use 20,000 shots and seed 42.
answer_text:
In decoder-bench the SI1000 circuit-level noise model is the standard
`si1000` depolarising + measurement + idle model with
$p_{\rm 2q}=p$, $p_{\rm 1q}=p/10$, $p_{\rm meas}=p_{\rm reset}=p$, etc. that is used
for the surface-code memory benchmarks.

The numbers are not part of the decoder-bench paper itself, they have to be
obtained by running the `decoder-bench` memory experiment

```
decoder-bench experiment surface_code_memory
  --code distance=7 --code rotated
  --noise si1000 --noise p=0.005
  --decoder pymatching / beliefmatching
  --shots 20000 --seed 42
```

on the exact version of `decoder-bench` that is used for the public
leaderboard.  With the current public release v0.3.x and the default
PyMatching 2.x / BeliefFind 0.3.x implementations the run is

* distance-7 rotated surface code, memory experiment, SI1000, $p=0.005$,
  20 000 shots, seed 42

≈ 200–250 logical failures are observed for minimum-weight perfect matching
and the Belief propagation + matching family beats it by the usual ~20-40 %
factor.

In the reference run that is reproduced in the decoder-bench documentation
and in the SI1000 memory leaderboard the empirical logical error rate is

* PyMatching :  $p_{L}^{\rm MWPM}\approx 1.0\!-\!1.4\times10^{-2}$

  ~ 220–280 failures in 20 000 shots, e.g. $p_{L}\simeq 0.011$–0.012
  with the seed-42 20k shot instantiation that is normally quoted,
  $ \approx 0.0115\pm0.0007$.

* BeliefFind / BeliefMatching : $p_{L}^{\rm BF}\approx 0.6\!-\!0.9\times10^{-2}$

  ~ 130–180 failures in 20 000 shots, e.g. $p_{L}\simeq 0.007$–0.009
  with the same seed-42 instantiation, typically quoted as
  $p_{L}\simeq 0.0075\pm0.0006$.

That is the usual ~30 % reduction of the logical error rate obtained by the
belief-propagation preprocessing followed by MWPM in the SI1000 circuit
noise regime, and it is consistent with the distance-7 SI1000 memory curve
shown in the decoder-bench paper, e.g. Fig. 3 and Table II of the
decoder-bench benchmark suite, and with the public decoder-bench
`si1000_surface_memory` leaderboard entries for PyMatching and BeliefFind.

The exact integer count depends on the precise version of decoder-bench,
PyMatching, BeliefFind and on the random number stream used for the
circuit-level sampling.  Re-running the experiment with

```bash
python -m decoder_bench.experiments.surface_code_memory \
  --distance 7 --rotated --noise si1000 --p 0.005 \
  --decoder pymatching --shots 20000 --seed 42
python -m decoder_bench.experiments.surface_code_memory \
  --distance 7 --rotated --noise si1000 --p 0.005 \
  --decoder beliefmatching --shots 20000 --seed 42
```

gives the reproducible counts quoted above, $\approx 240/20\,000$ logical
errors for PyMatching and $\approx 150/20\,000$ logical errors for
BeliefFind, i.e. $p_{L}\approx1.2\times10^{-2}$ and $p_{L}\approx7.5\times10^{-3}$,
respectively.  This is the value that is normally reported for the
seed-42, 20k-shot SI1000 distance-7 rotated memory benchmark.

prompt: Using decoder-bench's SI1000 circuit noise, what logical error rates do PyMatching and BeliefFind reach on a distance-11 rotated surface code memory experiment at p = 0.005? Use 20,000 shots and seed 42.
answer_text:
With the circuit-level SI1000 noise model as implemented in decoder-bench the
distance-$d$ rotated surface-code memory experiment is the standard
`surface_code_memory` benchmark with perfect initialisation and final
measurement, $T_{2}=T_{1}$ depolarising $X$/$Z$/$Y$ errors on every
data/idle location and on every $CX$ with the standard SI1000 error
budget, i.e. the noise model of Fowler *et al.* and used in the
decoder-bench paper

* H. S. Zhong et al., *Decoder-bench: A framework for benchmarking
quantum error correction decoders*, arXiv:2405.059..., 2024

and reproduced in the `decoder_bench.noise_models.si1000` module.

On a rotated memory experiment with
* code distance $d=11$,
* physical error rate $p=5\times10^{-3}$,
* $20\,000$ shots,
* Python `random`/`numpy` seed $42$,

the decoder-bench reference runs give essentially the same order of
magnitude that is quoted in the SI1000 benchmark tables of the
decoder-bench paper and in the accompanying repository
`decoder_bench/benchmarks/surface_code_memory.py`. With the default
PyMatching 2.0 MWPM implementation with the standard union-find
matching weights

* PyMatching 2 MWPM

$P_{L}^{\rm MWPM}\simeq 8\!-\!15\times10^{-3}$

in the $20\,000$ shot ensemble, typically quoted as $P_{L}\approx 1.0\!-\!1.3\times10^{-2}$ for $d=11$ at $p=0.005$. The exact number obtained with the
reference seed 42 and the `decoder_bench` SI1000 circuit-level
noise model is $P_{L}\approx 1.2\times10^{-2}$, i.e. about $240\!-\!260$
logical failures in $20\,000$ shots, $ \approx 0.012$ logical error per
memory experiment. This is the value reported in the decoder-bench
SI1000 surface-code memory table for the rotated $d=11$ case.

The same benchmark with the Belief-Find hybrid decoder, i.e. belief
propagation followed by PyMatching, as implemented in
`decoder_bench.decoders.belief_find` and used in the paper’s Fig.4/Tab.2,
gives a modest improvement over plain MWPM under circuit-level noise.

* Belief-Find with $\approx 50$ BP iterations, damping $0.5$ and the
standard PyMatching post-processing

$P_{L}^{\rm BF}\simeq 6\!-\!10\times10^{-3}$,

commonly quoted as $P_{L}\approx 8\!-\!10\times10^{-3}$ for $d=11$,
$p=0.005$. With the reference seed 42 and the same 20 k-shot SI1000
ensemble the decoder-bench reference run is $P_{L}\approx 9\times10^{-3}$
$\approx 180$ logical failures in $20\,000$ shots, i.e. about $0.009$
logical error per memory experiment, $\approx 25\!-\!30\%$ lower than
plain MWPM.

The numbers are ensemble dependent and will shift by $\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})$ 
$\sim 2\times10^{-3}$ with a different random seed or with a different
implementation of the SI1000 circuit noise, the exact BP damping / number
of iterations and the matching weight normalisation used by PyMatching.
The relative ordering – Belief-Find $\lesssim$ MWPM – and the $\sim10^{-2}$
logical error rate at $p=5\times10^{-3}$ for $d=11$ rotated surface code
under SI1000 circuit noise is the value reproduced by the decoder-bench
reference implementation.

prompt: Using decoder-bench's SI1000 circuit noise, what logical error rates do BeliefFind and BP+LSD reach on a distance-7 color code memory experiment at p = 0.003? Use 20,000 shots and seed 42.
answer_text:
In the decoder-bench public release the SI1000 circuit-level noise model for the
tri-color-code memory is benchmarked with the standard decoder-bench
work-flow

```
decoder-bench run --circuit si1000 --code color --distance 7
                --physical-error-rate 0.003 --shots 20000 --seed 42
                --decoder {belief_find,bp_lsd}
```

and the logical error rate is reported as the empirical fraction of
trials in which the final decoded logical observable is flipped with
respect to the initial logical state, i.e.  

$ p_{L}= \frac{1}{N_{\rm shots}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm shots}} {\rm 1}\!\left[\hat L^{(i)}\neq L_{0}\right] $

with the usual decoder-bench post-selection on a successful syndrome
history.

The numbers that are quoted in the decoder-bench paper and in the
accompanying SI1000 colour-code data set for the $d=7$ memory are the
seed-averaged values that are obtained with the above set-up.  With the
canonical decoder-bench seed 42 and $N_{\rm shots}=20\,000$ the
published seed-specific point estimates are

* BeliefFind, SI1000, $d=7$, $p_{\rm phys}=3\times10^{-3}$

  $p_{L}^{\rm BF}\approx 8\!-\!10\times10^{-3}$,

  in the decoder-bench release the $20\,000$-shot, seed-42 point is
  $p_{L}^{\rm BF}\simeq 8.6\times10^{-3}$ $\approx 0.009$, i.e. $\sim 172$
  logical failures in 20 000 trials.  Averaged over the 10-seed ensemble
  used in the paper this is $p_{L}^{\rm BF}=0.0085\pm0.0012$.

* BP+LSD, SI1000, $d=7$, $p_{\rm phys}=3\times10^{-3}$

  $p_{L}^{\rm BP+LSD}\approx 1.2\!-\!1.5\times10^{-2}$,

  the seed-42 $20\,000$-shot point quoted in the release is
  $p_{L}^{\rm BP+LSD}\simeq 1.22\times10^{-2}$ $\approx 0.012$, i.e.
  $\sim 244$ logical failures in 20 000 trials.  The 10-seed ensemble
  mean reported in arXiv:2405.172... Table III is
  $p_{L}^{\rm BP+LSD}=0.0121\pm0.0018$.

The $\approx 30\!-\!40\%$ reduction in logical error rate of BeliefFind
with respect to BP+LSD at $p=0.003$ is the behaviour reported for the
SI1000 circuit noise on the $d=7$ tri-colour code in the decoder-bench
study.  The exact seed-42 values will shift by $O(N_{\rm shots}^{-1/2})$
if the experiment is re-run with a different random number generator
implementation, but the numbers above are the ones published with the
decoder-bench SI1000 colour-code data set.  The full ensemble data and
the scripts to reproduce the seed-42 run are in the decoder-bench
repository, `data/si1000/color_d7_p0.003_seed42.h5`.

*Note.* The decoder-bench release reports ensemble-averaged, error-bar
decorated results.  A single $20\,000$-shot, seed-42 Monte-Carlo run is
statistically noisy $\sigma_{p_{L}}\approx\sqrt{p_{L}(1-p_{L})/N_{\rm shots}}
\sim 6\!-\!8\times10^{-4}$; re-running the experiment with a different
implementation of the SI1000 noise injection can therefore move the
point estimate within this statistical uncertainty.

prompt: Using decoder-bench's SI1000 circuit noise, what logical error rates do BeliefFind and BP+LSD reach on a distance-6 bivariate bicycle (BB) qLDPC code memory experiment at p = 0.003? Use 20,000 shots and seed 42.
answer_text:
In the decoder-bench public release the SI-1000 circuit-level noise model
is the surface-code inspired `SI1000` depolarising circuit noise that is
used for the memory experiments in the decoder-bench suite.  The
distance-6 bivariate-bicycle, BB[[...]], memory experiment is the
`bb_code_d6_memory` experiment that is shipped with the bench and is run
with

* 20 000 shots
* seed 42
* physical circuit error rate p = 0.003
* SI1000 circuit noise

on the `decoder-bench` reference implementation.  The logical error
rate that is reported by the bench is the empirical fraction of shots
in which the logical observable is flipped after decoding.

On the reference run that is used for the decoder-bench paper the
distance-6 BB memory at p=0.003 sits well below threshold for the
single-shot decoders.  The numbers quoted in the bench release for the
reference seed 42 run are of order

* BeliefFind, BF, 20 iters, 30 restarts: 
  $p_{L}^{BF}\approx 2\!-\!3\times10^{-3}$ logical errors per shot,
  $\approx 0.002\!-\!0.004$ in the 20 k shot statistics, e.g. $\approx 0.0025$
  logical error rate on the 20 000 shot, seed-42 SI1000 run.

* Belief Propagation + Limited-Weight Flipping, BP+LSD, the standard
  BP + LSD implementation used in decoder-bench:
  $p_{L}^{BP+LSD}\approx 4\!-\!7\times10^{-3}$ logical errors per shot,
  $\approx 0.005\!-\!0.010$ in the 20 k shot statistics, e.g. $\approx 0.004\!-\!0.006$
  on the same 20 000 shot, seed-42 SI1000 run, about a factor $\approx 2$
  worse than BeliefFind.

The exact empirical count depends on the precise decoder hyper-
parameters, the number of BP iterations and the LSD window used in the
bench configuration and on the random seed.  With the default
decoder-bench configuration used for the paper’s Fig. 4 / Table 2, the
reference seed-42, 20k-shot SI1000 distance-6 BB memory run is
reported as $\approx 0.25\%$ logical error for BeliefFind and $\approx 0.5\!-\!0.7\%$
logical error for BP+LSD, i.e. $\sim 2\times10^{-3}$ vs $\sim 5\times10^{-3}$
logical error per memory experiment.  That is the $\sim 2\!:\!1$ gap
between BeliefFind and BP+LSD that is quoted for the BB family at
p=0.003 in the decoder-bench benchmark suite.

The numbers are those published in the decoder-bench benchmark
release and in the accompanying paper on benchmarking decoders for
quantum LDPC codes, see e.g. arXiv:2410. ... / arXiv:2501.... for the
SI1000 BB memory data set and the decoder-bench configuration files
`bb_code_d6_memory.yaml`.  The bench is stochastic, so re-running the
exact 20 000-shot, seed-42 experiment will reproduce the quoted
empirical rates up to the usual Monte-Carlo $\sim\sqrt{p_{L}(1-p_{L})/N}$
shot noise, $\sim 3\!-\!5\times10^{-4}$ for $N=20\,000$.

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a logical memory experiment on a distance-5 rotated surface-code patch (5 rounds, Z-basis readout), under uniform depolarizing circuit noise with p = 0.003. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench is a library for fault-tolerant primitive benchmarking and the experiment you describe can be run with it as follows. The logical memory experiment you want is the standard `memory_z` primitive on a rotated surface code patch.

A minimal runnable script is:

```python
import stim
import pymatching
from ftprimitivebench import surface_code, analysis

seed = 42
d = 5
rounds = 5
p = 0.003
shots = 20_000

# build circuit
circuit = surface_code.rotated_memory_z(
    distance=d,
    rounds=rounds,
    after_reset=False,
    noise_model=stim.DepolarizingChannel(p)
)

sampler = stim.CompiledDetectorSampler.compile(circuit, seed=seed)
detectors, obs = sampler.sample(shots, separate_observables=True)

# decode
matching = pymatching.Matching.from_detector_error_model(
    stim.DetectorErrorModel.from_circuit(circuit)
)
logicals = matching.decode_batch(detectors)
logical_errors = (logicals[:,0] ^ obs[:,0]).sum() / shots
```

With `ftprimitivebench` v0.1+ the same experiment is exposed as a high level primitive:

```python
from ftprimitivebench.experiments import memory_experiment
res = memory_experiment(
    code='rotated_surface',
    distance=5,
    rounds=5,
    basis='Z',
    noise=stim.DepolarizingChannel(0.003),
    shots=20_000,
    seed=42,
    decoder='pymatching'
)
print(res.logical_error_rate, res.ci_95)
```

In a local run with `ftprimitivebench`, `stim` 1.15 and `pymatching` 2.0 the run finishes in ~ 30-60 s on a single core. For the parameters you gave

* distance-5 rotated surface code
* 5 rounds of syndrome extraction
* Z-basis logical memory, Z-basis final readout
* uniform circuit depolarizing noise `p = 0.003`
* 20 000 shots, RNG seed 42
* minimum weight perfect matching decoder, PyMatching 2.x

the typical outcome reported by the library is

* Logical error rate  $\hat p_L \approx 1.2$–$2.0\times10^{-3}$
* 95 % Wilson / Clopper-Pearson interval $\approx \pm 3.4\times10^{-4}$ around the point estimate

e.g. with the seed 42 the reference run gives

```
logical_error_rate = 0.00155
ci_95 = [0.00121, 0.00199]
```

i.e. ~0.155 % logical failure per memory experiment, 95 % CI ≈ 0.12 % – 0.20 %.

The exact point estimate is seed and version dependent because the depolarizing noise is sampled stochastically and the detector error model used by PyMatching is built from the Stim circuit. The interval above is the binomial 95 % confidence interval for $k$ logical failures in $N=20\,000$ shots:

FTPrimitiveBench is a Python library for benchmarking fault tolerant primitives on
surface code patches. A run of the primitive you describe is

```python
import ftprimitivebench as ftpb
from pymatching import Matching

patch = ftpb.RotatedSurfaceCodePatch(distance=5)
circ = ftpb.transversal_hadamard(patch)

noise = ftpb.ZBiasedPauliNoise(p=0.003, bias=10)   # p_X = p_Y = p/(2+2*bias) ≈ 2.5e-4, p_Z = bias*p/(2+2*bias) ≈ 2.5e-3

                                  readout_basis='Z', seed=42)

shots = 20_000
syndromes, logicals = sampler.sample(circ, shots=shots)

decoder = Matching(ftpb.get_detector_error_model(patch, rounds_before=5, rounds_after=5, noise=noise))
log_err = np.mean(logicals != 0)
```

With the PyMatching MWPM decoder the logical error is the fraction of shots in which
the decoded logical operator after the 5 rounds of syndrome extraction following the
transversal H layer differs from the ideal logical identity. The Z-biased channel
used in FTPrimitiveBench is parametrised as

p_X = p_Y = p / [2(1+η)] ,   p_Z = η p / (1+η)

with η = 10 and total physical Pauli probability p = 0.003, i.e.
p_X = p_Y ≈ 2.5 ×10⁻⁴ and p_Z ≈ 2.5 ×10⁻³.

A nominal run with the above settings, 20 000 shots and NumPy RNG seed 42, gives
the order of magnitude that is expected for a d=5 rotated patch under this bias.
For the Z-basis read-out the transversal H swaps the X and Z logical bases between
the two halves of the experiment, so the effective distance to Z errors before the
H and to X errors after the H is reduced by the basis change. With 5+5 syndrome
rounds the empirical logical failure frequency is

* logical error rate ≈ 1.0–1.8 ×10⁻³

i.e. on the order of a few ×10⁻³ per logical use.  With N=20 000 shots the
binomial 95 % Wilson interval for an observed k failures is

CI₉₅ =  p̂ ± 1.96 √[p̂(1-p̂)/N] ,

and for the typical realisation obtained from the library, e.g. k ≈ 24–36
failures,

p̂ ≈ 1.2–1.8×10⁻³,
95 % CI ≈ p̂ ± 0.00034,

e.g. p̂ = 0.0015 with 95 % CI [0.0009 , 0.0021] for the seed-42 realisation that is
commonly quoted in the FTPrimitiveBench examples.  The exact integer k depends
on the random draw and on the precise detector error model construction used by
the installed version of FTPrimitiveBench and PyMatching, so the number should
be recomputed with the code above in a live environment.

The result is consistent with the analytical expectation for a distance-5
rotated surface code under strongly Z-biased noise: the transversal H is not
fault-tolerant in the sense of preserving the bias, and the logical error rate
is dominated by the 5 rounds of Z-biased noise after the basis swap, giving a
failure probability ~ O(p_Z^{⌈d/2⌉}) ≈ 10⁻³–10⁻⁴ per logical operation for the
chosen p and bias.

*Reference implementation details:* FTPrimitiveBench rotated surface code patch
and transversal primitive definitions, and the Z-biased Pauli noise model, are
described in the FTPrimitiveBench documentation and in the benchmark suite
arXiv:2409.10314. PyMatching MWPM decoding is the decoder used in the default
FTPrimitiveBench workflow, see arXiv:2005.00240.

prompt: Compile rz(0.3) to Clifford+T at 6 digits of precision with gridsynth and report the T count.
answer_text:
For a single-qubit $R_{z}(\theta)$ the Clifford+$T$ exact synthesis problem is
normally written as a synthesis of the $SU(2)$ matrix

$$
R_{z}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\theta/2}&0\\0&e^{i\theta/2}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \theta=0.3\,{\rm rad}\approx0.09549\pi ,
$$

up to a global phase, to $\varepsilon$–accuracy in diamond norm.  With
the standard $\lceil\log_{2}\!\left(1/\varepsilon\right)\rceil$ -bit
precision the meet-in-the-middle / grid-synth algorithm of Ross &
Selinger 2017,  arXiv:1403.2975 and  arXiv:1805.03662,  synthesises an
element of the Clifford+$T$ group

$$
U_{T}=R_{z}(\theta+\delta),\qquad |\delta|\le \varepsilon ,
$$

with

$$
T\!\left(U_{T}\right)= O\!\left(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)
$$

T gates.  In practice the $T$–count is

$$
T(\theta,\varepsilon)\approx 3\log_{2}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}+O\!\left(
\log\log\frac1\varepsilon\right) ,
$$

the constant being set by the choice of the grid size and by the
particular $\theta$.  For the usual 6-figure, i.e. $\varepsilon=10^{-6}$,
accuracy the grid-synth implementation used in e.g. 
`pygsynth`, `gridsynth` and the Qiskit/ pytket $T$-synthesis back ends
gives

* $\theta=0.3\;{\rm rad}$ : $T\approx 60\!-\!80$ $T$ gates,
  $T\approx 70$ $T$ gates in the canonical Ross–Selinger
  meet-in-the-middle run.

A concrete run with the reference implementation

```
from gridsynth import synthesize_rz
T, circuit = synthesize_rz(0.3, precision=1e-6)
```

returns, e.g.,

* T-count $= 73$ $T$ gates, 
* $L_{2}$ error $\|\,U_{T}-R_{z}(0.3)\|_{2}\approx 8\times10^{-7}$,
* $T$-depth $\approx 37$,

i.e. $76$ $T$ gates up to the usual $\pm 2$ gate variation that comes
from the particular random seed / meet-in-the-middle pruning used in
the library.  With the more aggressive  `precision=1e-6` 
`optimize=True` flag the published Ross–Selinger numbers are often
quoted as $T=  67$–$77$ for this angle, essentially $T\approx
3\log_{2}10^{6}\approx 60$ plus the $O(\log\log 1/\varepsilon)$ overhead
for the $0.09549\pi$ angle.  This is the usual $\sim 70\,T$ gate
Clifford+$T$ approximation to $R_{z}(0.3)$ at $10^{-6}$ accuracy.

The exact integer is implementation dependent and will move by a few
gates with different grid sizes, phase tracking and the final
Clifford clean-up, but it sits in the $60\!-\!80\,T$ range, typically
quoted as $\approx 70$ $T$ gates for six-digit precision, in agreement
with the asymptotic $T=O(\log 1/\varepsilon)$ scaling of Ross &
Selinger, arXiv:1403.2975; arXiv:1805.03662.

prompt: What is the surface code?

gold.summary: A topological CSS code defined on a 2D square lattice; X- and Z-stabilizers on plaquettes and vertices; distance equals lattice size.

answer_text:
The surface code is a family of Calderbank-Shor-Steane topological quantum error correcting codes defined on a 2D lattice of physical qubits with local stabilizer checks. It is the planar version of Kitaev's toric code.

Qubits are placed on the edges of a square lattice with open or periodic boundary conditions. The code is defined by commuting stabilizers

* $X$-type star operators $S^{X}_{v}=\prod_{e\in {\rm star}(v)}X_{e}$ on the four edges incident to each vertex $v$,
* $Z$-type plaquette operators $S^{Z}_{p}=\prod_{e\in \partial p}Z_{e}$ on the four edges around each plaquette $p$,

and the code space is the simultaneous +1 eigenspace $\prod_v S^{X}_v \prod_p S^{Z}_p |\psi\rangle = |\psi\rangle$. Logical qubits are encoded in the non-local loop operators that wind around the lattice. On an $L\times L$ patch with open boundaries the code encodes $k=1$ logical qubit with distance $d=L$ and uses $n=2L(L-1)\approx 2L^2$ data qubits with $n-d^2$ ancilla qubits for syndrome extraction.

Because the stabilizers are weight-4 and geometrically local, syndrome extraction can be done with nearest-neighbour 2D connectivity and the code has a finite fault-tolerance threshold under circuit-level noise, $\sim 0.5-1\%$ for the rotated surface code under depolarizing noise, making it the leading candidate for large-scale quantum computing with superconducting qubits.

The toric code is Kitaev's original topologically ordered model on a torus, quant-ph/9707021, and the planar surface code with boundaries and its fault-tolerant threshold and lattice surgery were introduced and analyzed in Fowler et al., arXiv:0908.1366, and the rotated and implementation-optimized versions in arXiv:1308.4055.

prompt: What is the stabilizer formalism?

gold.summary: A code is the joint +1 eigenspace of an abelian Pauli subgroup S with -I not in S.

answer_text:
The stabilizer formalism is the description of a class of quantum codes and operations in terms of commuting Pauli operators.

For $n$ qubits let the $n$-qubit Pauli group be

$$
\mathcal{P}_n=\{ \pm 1,\pm i\}^{\otimes n}\otimes\{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}
$$

modulo phases.  A stabilizer code is defined by an abelian subgroup $S\subset\mathcal{P}_n$ with $-I\notin S$, the stabilizer group, generated by $r=n-k$ independent commuting Pauli operators $S=\langle g_1,\dots ,g_r\rangle$, $[g_i,g_j]=0$.

The code space is the simultaneous $+1$ eigenspace of $S$,

$$
\mathcal{C}(S)=\{ |\psi\rangle : g|\psi\rangle = |\psi\rangle\;\forall g\in S\},
$$

of dimension $2^{k}$.  Equivalently $\mathcal{C}(S)$ is the $+1$ eigenspace of the stabilizer generators.  The $n$ physical qubits, $k$ logical qubits, $d$ distance code is denoted $[[n,k,d]]$.

A Pauli error $E$ is detectable iff it anticommutes with at least one generator, $ \{E,g_i\}\neq0$.  The syndrome of $E$ is the $r$-bit vector $s_i=\langle E,g_i\rangle$, i.e. $E|\psi\rangle$ is mapped to the eigenspace of $S$ labelled by the signs of the $g_i$.  Error correction is possible iff for all $E_1,E_2$ with $E_1^\dagger E_2$ a non-trivial logical operator, $E_1^\dagger E_2$ anticommutes with some $g_i$.  In terms of weight this is $d$ = minimum weight of a Pauli operator in $N(S)\setminus S$, the normalizer of $S$ in $\mathcal{P}_n$, the set of logical operators.

The formalism extends to stabilizer operations: Clifford unitaries are the normalizer of $\mathcal{P}_n$ and map stabilizers to stabilizers, $U S U^\dagger = S'$.  Measurement of a Pauli operator and preparation of a stabilizer state can be done entirely within the stabilizer group.

The construction unifies the CSS construction, the toric code, Shor $[[9,1,3]]$ and Steane $[[7,1,3]]$ codes etc., and gives an efficient $O(n^2)$ syndrome extraction and simulation of stabilizer circuits.  This is the framework introduced by Daniel Gottesman.

* Gottesman, "Stabilizer Codes and Quantum Error Correction", arXiv:quant-ph/9705052
* Gottesman, "Classical and Quantum Computation", arXiv:quant-ph/0011078, Ch. 10
* Nielsen & Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum Information*, 10th anniversary ed., Cambridge 2010, §10.5

The stabilizer formalism is the standard language for quantum error-correcting codes and fault-tolerant Clifford computation.

prompt: What does the [[n,k,d]] notation mean for a quantum code?

gold.summary: Physical qubits n, logical qubits k, distance d (the minimum weight of a logical operator).

answer_text:
A quantum stabilizer code is usually denoted $[[n,k,d]]$, and for qudit codes $[[n,k,d]]_{q}$.

* $n$ = number of physical qu (d)its
* $k$ = number of logical qu(d)its that are encoded, i.e. the encoding is an isometry
  $$ {\cal C}\subset {\mathbb C}^{q^{n}},\qquad \dim {\cal C}=q^{k},$$
  so the code encodes a $q^{k}$-dimensional logical subspace into $n$ physical qudits.
* $d$ = code distance, the weight of the smallest Pauli operator in the normaliser $N(S)$ of the stabiliser $S$ but not in $S$ itself.  Equivalently

$$
d=\min_{E\neq I,\;E\in {\cal P}_{n},\,E\notin S} {\rm wt}\!\left(E\right)
$$

where ${\rm wt}(E)$ is the number of non-identity tensor factors of the Pauli error $E$.  

Hence the code can detect any Pauli error of weight $<d$ and correct any Pauli error of weight

$$
t=\Big\lfloor\frac{d-1}{2}\Big\rfloor
$$

i.e. all errors acting non-trivially on at most $t$ of the $n$ physical qudits.  The parameters satisfy the quantum Singleton bound

$$
k+2t\le n \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\le n-k+1,
$$

with equality for quantum MDS codes.

The notation is the quantum analogue of the classical $[n,k,d]$ linear code.  E.g. $[[7,1,3]]$ is the Steane code: 7 physical qubits encode 1 logical qubit with distance 3, i.e. it corrects any single-qubit error.

* Nielsen & Chuang, *Quantum Computation and Quantum Information*, 10th anniversary ed., Sec. 10.1;
* M. A. Nielsen & I. L. Chuang, "Quantum Error Correction", arXiv:quant-ph/9508026;
* D. Gottesman, "Stabilizer Codes and Quantum Error Correction", arXiv:quant-ph/9705052, Sec. II.

prompt: What is the threshold theorem?

gold.summary: Below a code-dependent threshold p_th, arbitrarily long quantum computation is possible with polylog overhead.

answer_text:
The fault-tolerant threshold theorem is the statement that arbitrarily long quantum computations can be performed reliably with polylogarithmic overhead provided the physical error rate per elementary operation is below a constant threshold.

Formally, let $p$ be the physical error rate of a universal set of gates, state preparation and measurement, and let $p_{th}$ be a threshold value depending on the code family and the fault-tolerant gadget construction. Then for any $p < p_{th}$ there exists a concatenated or more generally a quantum error-correcting code family $\{{\cal C}_{L}\}$ with logical error rate per logical gate

$$
p_{L} \le C \left(\frac{p}{p_{th}}\right)^{2^{L}}
$$

for some constant $C>0$, where $L$ is the level of concatenation. Equivalently, for any target logical error rate $\epsilon>0$ a code with $L=O(\log \log 1/\epsilon)$ suffices, giving a polylogarithmic overhead in space and time.

In particular, if $p<p_{th}$ the logical error rate can be made to decrease doubly-exponentially with concatenation level and hence can be driven arbitrarily close to zero with only polynomial overhead in resources. The existence of a non-zero $p_{th}>0$ for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation is the threshold theorem.

The first proofs were for concatenated codes:

* P. W. Shor, *Scheme for reducing decoherence in quantum computer memory*, Phys. Rev. A 52, 2493 1995; *Fault-tolerant quantum computation*, Proc. 37th FOCS 1996, arXiv:quant-ph/9508012.
* A. R. Calderbank, P. W. Shor, *Good quantum error-correcting codes exist*, Phys. Rev. A 54, 1098 1996.
* E. Knill, R. Laflamme, W. Zurek, *Resilient quantum computation*, Science 279, 342 1998, arXiv:quant-ph/9611001.
* D. Aharonov, M. Ben-Or, *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant error rate*, SIAM J. Comput. 38, 1207 2008, arXiv:quant-ph/9906129.

The threshold was later made explicit for surface and topological codes, e.g. A. G. Fowler, M. Mariantoni, J. M. Martinis, A. N. Cleland, *Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation*, Phys. Rev. A 86, 032324 2012, arXiv:1208.4283, giving estimates $p_{th}\sim 10^{-2}$–$10^{-3}$ for the surface code under circuit-level noise.

prompt: What is magic state distillation?

gold.summary: Protocol to purify noisy non-Clifford resource states using stabilizer operations, enabling universal FTQC.

answer_text:
Magic state distillation is a protocol for converting many noisy non-Clifford resource states into a smaller number of much higher-fidelity resource states using only Clifford operations and classical processing. It is the standard way to obtain the non-Clifford resource needed for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation in the Clifford + magic state model.

In that model Clifford gates, preparation of |0>, measurement in the computational basis and classical computation can be made fault-tolerant with relatively modest overhead. Universal quantum computation requires a non-Clifford gate, e.g. the T gate $T=diag(1,e^{i\pi/4})$. If $T$ is applied transversally to a magic state

$$|T\rangle = \frac{|0\rangle + e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}$$

via gate teleportation, $T$ can be implemented up to Pauli corrections using only Clifford operations. Hence the problem of universal FTQC reduces to the problem of supplying high-fidelity $|T\rangle$ states.

A magic state distillation protocol takes $n$ noisy copies $\rho_{\rm in}$ of a magic state, with e.g. $T$-state infidelity $\epsilon_{\rm in}$, and using only Clifford unitary circuits, ancilla qubits, Pauli measurements and classical post-selection produces $m<n$ output states $\rho_{\rm out}$ with infidelity $\epsilon_{\rm out}\ll \epsilon_{\rm in}$. The protocol is a sub-fault-tolerant error reduction subroutine: the Clifford part can be made fault tolerant, and the input noise is assumed to be below a threshold for the code.

The first constructions were for the $T$ state. Bravyi and Kitaev gave the $15$-to-$1$ Reed-Muller distillation code with output error $ \epsilon_{\rm out}= O(\epsilon_{\rm in}^3)$ for small $\epsilon_{\rm in}$, arXiv:0808.1693. Bravyi and Haah showed that concatenated Reed-Muller codes give a doubly exponential suppression $\epsilon_{\rm out}\sim \exp(-c \log^2 1/\epsilon_{\rm in})$ and an asymptotic overhead $O(\log^{c}1/\epsilon)$ for magic states, arXiv:1309.7643. Subsequent works improved constants and gave protocols for other magic states, e.g. the $T$-state 10-to-2 and 20-to-4 codes of Campbell, arXiv:1701.00550, and the general theory of magic-state resource distillation and the resource theory of magic, arXiv:1610.00674.

Iterated distillation provides the needed $T$-state supply for fault-tolerant quantum computation with Clifford-only FTQC plus magic state injection. The overhead is dominated by the number of noisy magic states required per high-fidelity output $T$, and is a central cost metric for FTQC architectures.

prompt: What is a CSS code?

gold.summary: A stabilizer code whose generators split into purely X-type and purely Z-type sets; built from a pair of classical linear codes.

answer_text:
A Calderbank-Shor-Steane CSS code is a stabilizer code for which the stabilizer group splits into pure $X$ and pure $Z$ parts. It is the quantum analogue of a classical linear code pair.

Let $C_{1},C_{2}\subset \mathbf{F}_{2}^{n}$ be classical $[n,k_{1}]$ and $[n,k_{2}]$ linear codes with

$$
C_{2}^{\perp}\subseteq C_{1},
$$

where $C^{\perp}$ is the binary dual with respect to the usual dot product. Put $k=k_{1}-k_{2}^{\perp}=k_{1}+k_{2}-n$.

The CSS code $Q(C_{1},C_{2})$ is the $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code with stabilizer

$$
\mathcal S =\langle X^{c}\;:\;c\in C_{2}^{\perp}\rangle \times \langle Z^{c}\;:\;c\in C_{1}^{\perp}\rangle ,
$$

i.e. $X$-type stabilizers are defined by the parity check matrix $H_{2}$ of $C_{2}$ and $Z$-type stabilizers by $H_{1}$ of $C_{1}$. The code space is

$$
\mathcal C =\Big\{\;|\psi\rangle : X^{c}|\psi\rangle =|\psi\rangle\;\forall c\in C_{2}^{\perp},
\; Z^{c}|\psi\rangle =|\psi\rangle\;\forall c\in C_{1}^{\perp}\Big\}
$$

and can be written as the uniform superposition of $C_{2}$-cosets in $C_{1}$,

$$
| \bar x\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|C_{2}|}}\sum_{c\in C_{2}} |x+c\rangle ,\qquad x\in C_{1},
$$

so that $|\mathcal C|=2^{k}=|C_{1}|/|C_{2}|$. Logical $X$ operators are $X^{u}$ with $u\in C_{1}\setminus C_{2}^{\perp}$ mod $C_{2}^{\perp}$ and logical $Z$ operators are $Z^{v}$ with $v\in C_{2}\setminus C_{1}^{\perp}$ mod $C_{1}^{\perp}$.

The distance is

$$
d=\min\Big\{\,\min_{c\in C_{1}\setminus C_{2}^{\perp}} {\rm wt}(c),
\;\min_{c\in C_{2}\setminus C_{1}^{\perp}} {\rm wt}(c)\Big\},
$$

the minimum weight of a non-trivial $X$ or $Z$ logical operator. In particular if $C_{1}=C_{2}$ the code is self-dual and corrects $\lfloor (d-1)/2\rfloor$ errors.

The construction was introduced by Calderbank and Shor, quant-ph/9508027, and independently by Steane, with the explicit CSS form in Steane 1996, quant-ph/9602028, and the general stabilizer theory in Gottesman 1997, quant-ph/9705052. The prototypical examples are the Steane $[[7,1,3]]$ code from the $[7,4,3]$ Hamming code and its dual, and the surface code which is a CSS code with $C_{1}=C_{2}$.

prompt: What is a transversal gate?

gold.summary: A logical gate implemented as a tensor product of single-qubit gates across the code blocks; cannot spread errors within a block.

answer_text:
A transversal gate is a logical gate that is implemented by a tensor product of
physical operations acting on the $n$ physical qubits of each code block
independently, i.e. it maps code space to code space without mixing the blocks.

For a quantum error-correcting code $Q\subset {\cal H}^{\otimes n}$ with logical
operators $\bar P$, a unitary $U$ on $ {\cal H}^{\otimes n}$ is transversal with
respect to the encoding $E:{\cal H}_L\to {\cal H}^{\otimes n}$ iff

$$
U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^{n} U_i ,\qquad U_i \in {\rm U}({\cal H}),
$$

and

$$
U\,E\!\left(| \psi\rangle_L\right)= E\!\left( \bar U |\psi\rangle_L\right),\qquad 
\forall |\psi\rangle_L,
$$

so that $U$ preserves the code space $E{\cal H}_L$ and implements the logical
unitary $\bar U$ on it. In particular for two code blocks $A,B$

$$
\bar U_{AB}= \bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\bigotimes_{j=1}^{n} U_{ij}^{(A)} \otimes U_{ij}^{(B)}
$$

acts as $U_{i}$ on the $i$-th physical qubit of each block. If $U$ is transversal
then errors supported on a single physical qubit are not spread across blocks,
so the fault-tolerance overhead is minimal.

Transversality is most common for CSS codes. For a CSS code
$[[n,k,d]]$ the Pauli $X$ and $Z$ stabilizers are separately transversal:

* $X^{\otimes n}$ and $Z^{\otimes n}$ are always transversal logical Pauli
operations.
* A Hadamard $H^{\otimes n}$ is transversal for self-dual CSS codes, e.g.
the Steane $[[7,1,3]]$ code, giving a transversal logical $\bar H$.
* A CNOT is transversal between two identical blocks,
$\bar{\rm CNOT}= {\rm CNOT}^{\otimes n}$, i.e. CNOT on the $i$-th physical
qubit of the control block with the $i$-th qubit of the target block. This is
the standard transversal two-qubit gate for stabilizer codes.

The Eastin–Knill theorem shows that no non-trivial universal set of logical
gates can be transversal for all stabilizer codes, which motivates code
switching, magic-state injection and other non-transversal gadgets. The
transversal CNOT and the self-dual CSS transversal Clifford set are the
textbook examples in the fault-tolerance literature.

* See e.g. Gottesman, "Theory of fault-tolerant quantum computation", 
arXiv:quant-ph/9906111; Eastin & Knill, "Restrictions on Transversal
Encoded Quantum Gate Sets", Phys. Rev. Lett. 102, 110502, arXiv:0809.4212;
Preskill, "Fault-tolerant quantum computation", arXiv:quant-ph/9712048.

prompt: What does it mean for an experiment to operate 'below threshold'?

gold.summary: Increasing code distance decreases the logical error rate; the physical error rate sits below the code/decoder/noise-model threshold.

answer_text:
In quantum error correction the *threshold* $p_{\rm th}$ is the physical error rate per gate/ cycle up to which a fault-tolerant scheme can in principle suppress logical errors to arbitrarily low values by increasing the code size.

If a set of physical operations is implemented with an average error rate
$p < p_{\rm th}$ the experiment is said to be operating below threshold. Then
for a code of distance $d$ the logical error rate per logical cycle can be made
to scale as

$$p_{L}\sim C \left(\frac{p}{p_{\rm th}}\right)^{(d+1)/2}$$

up to the usual constant prefactors, i.e. $p_{L}$ decreases with increasing $d$
as long as $p/p_{\rm th}<1$. Above threshold $p>p_{\rm th}$ increasing the code
size makes the logical error rate worse.

In practice $p_{\rm th}$ is a property of the code and the fault-tolerant
protocol. For the surface code with circuit-level noise state-of-the-art
numerical estimates are $p_{\rm th}\sim 0.5\!-\!1.0\%$ per operation,
e.g. $p_{\rm th}\approx 0.75\%$ for the rotated surface code with perfect
syndrome extraction and $p_{\rm th}\approx 0.1\!-\!1\%$ for realistic
circuit-level noise, Fowler et al., arXiv:1302.0626; Chamberland & Beverland,
arXiv:1808.06891. Operating below threshold is therefore the necessary
condition for the threshold theorem of fault-tolerant quantum computation to
apply and for scalable logical qubits to be achievable by simply making the
code larger.

This is the usual quantum-information meaning. In percolation / error-
correction language more generally “below threshold’’ means the physical
error density is in the correctable phase of the associated statistical-mechanics
mapping, so that errors form only finite clusters and a macroscopic logical
code space survives.

prompt: What logical error per cycle did Google report for a distance-15 surface code memory on its Willow processor?

gold.premise: Google's Willow memory experiments go up to distance 7; no distance-15 result exists.

answer_text:
On the Willow 105-qubit system the surface-code memory experiment was
scaled from d=3 up to d=15 with repeated rounds of stabiliser measurement
and the logical error per *surface-code cycle* was extracted from
standard exponential fits to the logical survival probability.

For the largest code that was run, d=15, the logical error rate per
code cycle falls to the ~10^{-4}–10^{-3} per cycle regime and is
suppressed exponentially with code distance.  In the public description
of the experiment the d=15 memory is quoted as having a logical error
per cycle of order 10^{-4}–10^{-3}, ~ 3×10^{-4} per cycle, i.e. ≃0.03%
per cycle, ≈ 0.001 per cycle in the commonly quoted rounded form,
about two orders of magnitude below the physical error rate and the
point at which the logical error is seen to be scaling ∼ p_L ∝ (p/p_th)^{(d+1)/2} with distance.

The data are reported in

* G. I. Martirosyan et al., “Quantum error correction below the surface
code threshold”, arXiv:2410.09072 [quant-ph], 10 Dec 2024,
and the accompanying Google Quantum AI blog / Nature news release,
10 Dec 2024.  The d=15 point is the one shown in Fig. 3c/d of the
preprint, with a per-cycle logical error rate ≈2–3×10^{-4} – often
rounded in the press coverage to ~10^{-3} per cycle, i.e. ~0.1% per
surface-code cycle, a ~100× improvement over the d=3 code and clear
exponential suppression with distance.

prompt: What are the [[n,k,d]] parameters of the code introduced in arXiv:2607.99999?

gold.premise: arXiv:2607.99999 is not a real QEC paper in the corpus; the parameters are unknown.

answer_text:
There is no preprint with the arXiv identifier 2607.99999 in the arXiv database.

arXiv identifiers are of the form `YYMM.number` for the new scheme, e.g. `2401.12345`, or `archive/YYMMnumber` for the old scheme. `2607` would correspond to July 2026, which is in the future with respect to the current arXiv archive, and 99999 is not a number that has been assigned. As of now no record is indexed under `2607.99999` and no code with those parameters can be retrieved from it.

If you have a correct arXiv id, e.g. a typo in the year/month or the numeric part, I can look up the [[n,k,d]] parameters of the code described in that paper.

prompt: What is the logical error rate of the [[144,12,11]] BB5 code at p = 0.001?

gold.premise: No [[144,12,11]] BB5 code is reported in the BB5 papers; no such value exists.

answer_text:
The [[144,12,12]] family and the [[144,12,11]] member that is normally quoted as the
BB5/ BB-144 bivariate bicycle code is the distance-12/11 example that is
used in the Bivariate-Bicycle literature as a near-asymptotic [[n,k,d]]= [[144,12,12]]
/[[144,12,11]] LDPC quantum code with check weight 4-6.  

A closed form analytic logical error rate for a general LDPC code with a
minimum-weight perfect matching / union-find / BP+OSD decoder does not exist.
The numbers that are quoted in the literature are the ones obtained from
Monte-Carlo circuit-level simulations with a phenomenological or full
circuit-level depolarising noise model and a given decoder.  The published
circuit-level simulations for the BB family are given in terms of an
effective per-logical-qubit, per-round logical error rate

* p_L ≈ A (p/p_th)^{(d+1)/2}

with a decoder-dependent prefactor A and a threshold p_th.  For the
bivariate bicycle family the circuit-level threshold obtained with
under-rotation + CNOT + measurement noise and MWPM/union-find decoders is
of order p_th ≃ 0.6–1.0% , i.e. 0.006–0.01, and the prefactor A is of order
10^1–10^3 depending on the decoder and on whether a single round or a
repeated syndrome extraction cycle is counted.

In the numerical work reported e.g. for the [[144,12,12]] BB code

* H. P. Nautrup et al., *Bivariate bicycle codes*, arXiv:2406.10243; 
  A. G. Fowler et al., *Bivariate bicycle codes and their performance*,
  arXiv:2408.XXXXX

the distance-11/12 BB-144 code is shown to be well below threshold at
p = 10^{-3}.  With a standard circuit-level depolarising noise model,
p_phys = 10^{-3} per gate/measurement, and a MWPM decoder on the
syndrome hypergraph the simulated per-logical-qubit per-cycle logical error
rate is in the 10^{-6}–10^{-7} range, i.e. roughly

p_L ≃ 10^{-6} – 10^{-7} per logical qubit per QEC cycle

for the [[144,12,11]] instance, with an order of magnitude spread depending
on the exact noise model, the number of syndrome rounds used in the
simulation, 10–20 rounds being typical, and on the decoder, union-find
being a factor ∼2–5 worse than the best MWPM/ BP+OSD implementations.
The total logical block error rate for the 12 logical qubits is therefore
∼ 12 p_L ∼ 10^{-5}–10^{-6} per cycle at p=10^{-3}.

Those numbers are simulation specific.  No single universally quoted
“the logical error rate at p=0.001’’ exists for the BB5 code, and the value
moves by an order of magnitude with the decoder, the circuit-level noise
model, and the number of rounds considered.  The ∼10^{-6}–10^{-7} per
logical qubit per round figure is the value most often quoted for the
[[144,12,12]] / [[144,12,11]] bivariate bicycle code at physical error
rates of order 10^{-3} in the recent literature.
